questions.title: Why did the Second Circuit deem the fair‑use analysis sufficient to dismiss the copyright claim at the pleading stage?
questions.question_body: In Santos v. Kimmel the appellate court affirmed the district court’s Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal, stating that the fair‑use defense was “clearly established by the complaint.” I thought fair‑use determinations required factual development and a full evidentiary hearing. How can a court decide that a use is fair‑use purely on the pleadings, and what precedent allows such a dismissal?

questions.title: What does it mean that the “purpose and character” factor focuses on whether the use is "transformative" rather than the parties’ subjective intent?
questions.question_body: The opinion emphasizes that a reasonable observer, not the copyright holder or Kimmel’s intent, determines transformation. How is that reasonable‑observer standard applied in practice, especially when the original creator (Santos) claims the purpose of the work was the same as Kimmel’s parody? Are there specific tests or examples the court uses to evaluate this?

questions.title: How does preemption analysis work for state‑law contract claims in a copyright case?
questions.question_body: The court dismissed Santos’s breach‑of‑contract and breach‑of‑implied‑contract claims as preempted by the Copyright Act, but said it need not reach the merits because the claims were insufficient. What is the legal test for determining that a state‑law contract claim is preempted, and why did the court think Santos’s claims fell within that test?

questions.title: Why can a non‑signatory like Santos not enforce the Cameo Terms of Service against Kimmel?
questions.question_body: Santos alleged that Kimmel breached the Cameo platform’s Terms of Service, yet the court said Santos was not a party to that contract and Illinois law presumes against third‑party benefits. How does the “strong presumption against conferring benefits to non‑contracting third parties” operate, and are there any circumstances where a third party could still enforce such terms?

questions.title: What are the pleading requirements for a fraud (fraudulent inducement) claim under New York law?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes Santos’s fraud claim was dismissed because he failed to allege out‑of‑pocket loss. What specific elements must a plaintiff plead to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion for fraudulent inducement in New York, and how does the out‑of‑pocket loss requirement differ from other fraud elements?

questions.title: Can the market‑harm factor of fair‑use be satisfied when the secondary work is a parody that may actually increase interest in the original?
questions.question_body: The court said Santos did not suffer market harm because Kimmel’s segments were not a substitute for the original videos. In cases like Campbell v. Acuff‑Rose, courts sometimes find no market harm for parodies. How do courts assess the “effect on the potential market” when the secondary work could boost the original’s visibility or value?

questions.title: Does the fact that the videos were published on the same day they were created affect the fair‑use analysis?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions the copyright registrations showing the videos were published the same day they were created. How does the timing of publication influence the fair‑use factors, particularly the “nature of the copyrighted work” and the “amount and substantiality” factors?

questions.title: What is the significance of the court’s citation to Harper & Row’s “good‑faith” comment in modern fair‑use doctrine?
questions.question_body: The opinion discusses that the Supreme Court’s statement that fair use presumes good faith has been “distanced from” in later cases. How have courts treated the good‑faith requirement in recent fair‑use jurisprudence, and does bad‑faith conduct ever defeat a fair‑use defense?
